title: Energy Technologies
description: Generation roles, storage (batteries, pumped hydro, hydrogen), duration vs power, round-trip efficiency, and demand-side flexibility.

cards.front: Three questions that sort almost any energy technology?
cards.back: 1) **Can you control it?** (dispatchable vs variable). 2) **How fast can it change?** (ramp rate). 3) **Can it store energy, and for how long?** (power vs energy capacity / duration).

**CCGT** (combined-cycle) adds a steam turbine to recover exhaust heat → ~55–60% efficient, fairly flexible workhorse. **OCGT** (open-cycle) is a single turbine → less efficient but starts fast, so it's a peaker that often sets the price.

cards.front: A battery is rated **50 MW / 200 MWh**. For how long can it deliver full power?
cards.back: Duration $t = E/P = 200/50 = 4$ h. Power (MW) and energy (MWh) are rated separately; their ratio is the duration.

cards.front: What is **round-trip efficiency**, and rough values for Li-ion, pumped hydro, hydrogen?
cards.back: Energy out ÷ energy in over a charge–discharge cycle. **Li-ion ~85–95%**, **pumped hydro ~70–85%**, **hydrogen ~30–40%**. Lower = more loss per cycle.

cards.front: Why does hydrogen's low round-trip efficiency still make sense for some storage?
cards.back: Its ~30–40% efficiency would be ruinous for *daily* cycling, but it's acceptable for **long-duration / seasonal** storage that runs only a few times a year — where cheap energy capacity and long discharge matter more than per-cycle loss.

cards.front: Why is **pumped hydro** still ~95% of the world's storage?
cards.back: It's cheap per kWh, long-lived, and very large-scale — pump water uphill when power is cheap, release it through turbines when needed. Main limit: it needs the right **geography**.

cards.front: What is **inertia**, and why is it becoming a concern?
cards.back: Rotational kinetic energy in large synchronous generators that resists sudden frequency changes. Inverter-based wind/solar provide little of it, so as synchronous plants retire, frequency stability (and **grid-forming** inverters) becomes a real constraint.

cards.front: Match the storage duration to the right technology.
choices: Daily peaks → Li-ion; multi-day/seasonal lulls → hydrogen/thermal
cards.back: Match the *duration of the problem* to the *duration of the technology*: short frequent gaps suit fast batteries; long rare lulls suit hydrogen, thermal or CAES.

cards.front: What is **demand response**, and why is it valuable?
cards.back: Paying consumers (industry, EV charging, heat pumps, data centres) to shift or shed load at key moments — flexing demand to match supply. Often the **cheapest 'capacity'** on the system and a bridge to grid-and-compute.
Using (surplus) electricity to make other carriers — hydrogen, ammonia, synthetic fuels, heat. It soaks up cheap surplus power, links the grid to industry, and enables long-duration storage.
